name: Sunbeam
lede: Sunbeam is a soft, dusty gold recorded as a color name in 1917, and the thing it names, a shaft of sunlight in hazy air, is one of the hardest effects in painting.

sections.title: A color name with one source
sections.body:
Only one dictionary in our library lists *sunbeam* as a color, Maerz and Paul's of 1930, which dates it to 1917 and puts it on plate 11, square K 5; ISCC-NBS 1955 cites it and calls the swatch a dark yellow [2]. Who coined it, and for which fabric or paint, is undocumented in the books we hold.

Paterson's dictionary lists *sunbeam* only as the ray of light itself. The nearby entries *sunburn*, a color term he dates as early as 1590, and *sunflower*, a dark yellow, are marked as colors [1].

sections.title: What a sunbeam needs
sections.body:
Gurney, a painter who wrote a book on light, says a visible sunbeam needs three conditions: a high screen of cloud, foliage or architecture pierced by a few openings; air filled with dust, vapor or smoke; and a view toward the sun [3]. The rays are in fact parallel and only seem to converge on the sun in perspective [3]. Looking away from the sun they nearly vanish, because droplets scatter most light forward at small angles [3]. The beam also changes the shadows of the forms beyond it even more than their lit sides [3].

On canvas, he paints a beam by brushing a light, semiopaque tone over a dry background, or by premixing one string of colors for the lit air and another for the dark forest [3]. Opaque white alone makes the color chalky, so the chroma may have to be restored with a glaze [3]. He advises using sunbeams sparingly, since they draw the eye [3].

sections.title: Newton's sunbeam
sections.body: The most famous sunbeam in color science is Newton's [4]. In 1672 he darkened a room, made a small hole in the window shutter and put a prism in the beam that came through, which divided the white light into colors [4]. Livingstone adds that he found a beam's color to be a permanent property of that light [4].

sections.title: A flat tint, no glow
sections.body: The swatch, #E0C270, is a soft, slightly dusty gold with no glow in it [2]. Its nearest named neighbors are [[venetian-yellow]] (more vivid), [[reed-yellow]] (duller), [[popcorn]], [[ochre-yellow]] and [[brazen-yellow]], all within about 4 units [2]. The closest cut stone in our data is imperial or sherry [[gem:topaz|topaz]], about 8 units away [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 551 works, 2.3 per cent of the archive [5]. The six largest covers take up 65 to 81 per cent of the canvas, and they are grounds, not light: a Japanese fan album by Kanô Tsunenobu (1636), Kishi Ganku's [[painting:aic-92960|Bamboo]] (1801) and Indian paintings of about 1890 [5]. India has it in 73 of 721 works, 4.4 times the archive rate, and Kalighat paintings in 51 of 96 [5].

Inside a painting it is almost always among the lightest colors, in 97 per cent of cases, and it shares canvases with Khaki and Mustard far more than chance [5]. Among painters, [[painter:pierre-bonnard|Bonnard]] has it in 5 of 45 works and [[painter:joseph-mallord-william-turner|Turner]] in 3 of 14, small samples [5]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test [5].

questions.q: What does a painter need in the air to make a visible sunbeam, according to Gurney?
choices: Dust, vapor or smoke, and a view toward the sun
Perfectly clean air and the sun behind you
questions.answer: Dust, vapor or smoke, and a view toward the sun

questions.q: True or false: the rays of a sunbeam really converge on the sun.
What did Newton put in a beam of sunlight in 1672?

openers: A sunbeam is only visible because the air is full of dust or smoke: in clean air the light would pass unseen.
The rays in a sunbeam are parallel; they seem to meet at the sun only because of perspective.
Look for a sunbeam when you face the sun through a gap in clouds or leaves, never when you look away.

issues: Removed unsupported claim that a real beam is lighter/more saturated and that painters layer it
